edges.description: CCDC62 localises to the developing acrosome and interacts with GOPC, a Golgi protein required for proacrosomal vesicle transport; without CCDC62 acrosome formation is disrupted.
Failure of acrosome biogenesis produces round-headed, acrosome-less sperm.
Acrosome-less, dysmorphic sperm cannot fertilise the oocyte in vivo.
CCDC62 loss disrupts acrosome formation in spermatids, with deformed sperm, the mechanism proposed for the human disease.
edges.limitations: The human phenotype rests on a single proband; mouse spermiogenesis defects may be more complete than the human presentation, and acrosome ultrastructure was not compared directly across species.

nodes.description: There is no therapy that restores spermatogenesis. Acrosome-deficient (globozoospermic) sperm fail to fertilise oocytes naturally and often fail to activate the oocyte even after intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), because round-headed sperm lack normal oocyte-activating capacity. Artificial oocyte activation with a calcium ionophore is used to overcome this fertilisation failure, and a healthy live birth has been reported after calcium-ionophore activation of round-headed sperm. No ICSI/AOA outcome has been reported for a CCDC62-genotyped patient; the efficacy data come from general round-headed-sperm/globozoospermia populations, so this management is applied at the phenotype level. The globozoospermia case report (PMID:32318024) used a calcium ionophore without naming the specific compound; ionomycin is named here from the separate ionomycin-AOA study (PMID:41462321).

evidence.reference_title: Comparison of Human Oocyte Activation Between Round-Headed Sperm Injection Followed by Calcium Ionophore Treatment and Normal Sperm Injection in a Patient With Globozoospermia.
evidence.snippet: These results indicate that calcium ionophore treatment can assist oocyte activation in patients with round-headed sperm, but its efficiency to activate oocytes is lower than that induced by a normal sperm injection.

nodes.description: Loss of CCDC62 disrupts formation of the acrosome during spermiogenesis, producing malformed spermatids. In the mouse the acrosome fragments during the maturation phase of its development, and sperm show abnormal head bending with cytoplasm retained around the head. The acrosome is the Golgi-derived cap over the sperm head; its failure yields round-headed (globozoospermic) sperm.
